name: Rosa Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cleaning and hygiene supplies for a distributor that serves hospitals, schools and office cleaners. So it's bleach, paper towels, nitrile gloves, mop heads, hand soap by the pallet. Most of my day is on email and the phone, comparing quotes from about forty suppliers and making sure the hospitals never run out of gloves. I've been there four years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hospital side, because it feels like it matters. In the first winter of my job there was a glove shortage and I spent three days ringing factories to keep two hospitals stocked, and I've never been prouder. What grinds me down is the price chasing, because every quarter the suppliers push prices up and I have to fight it line by line.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat near the canal. I've got about eight months of pay saved, plus a little in an index fund my dad nagged me into. I use one of those AI chat tools sometimes to tidy up a tricky email to a supplier, but not every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful little tool and that's all, like spellcheck was. I'd probably say it's good the bosses can't use it as an excuse to cut people. I wouldn't post much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. A tool that saves me an hour a week doesn't change that I'm paid to negotiate and know which supplier will actually deliver. I'd keep what I've got and keep building on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the same way and keep using the chat tool for the odd difficult email. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into the index fund. Maybe I'd ask my manager about a senior buyer role next year, since nothing's shaking things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. It's a bit like the weather forecast saying no storm this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI tidies some of your emails now. In this picture, does anything about your week actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might write the first draft of the monthly price report, which takes me most of a Friday. That would be nice. I'd spend the Friday on the phone with suppliers instead, which is the part I'm actually good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture, even if AI does little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. My landlord put it up twice in two years, and I'd like to buy a flat before thirty. But that's an ordinary worry, not an AI one, and my savings cover me if anything goes wrong.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful little tool**, like spellcheck was.
I'd say it's good bosses can't use it as an **excuse to cut** people.
think: I'd be **fine**, because my job is negotiating and knowing which supplier really delivers.
Saving an **hour a week** doesn't change what I'm paid to do.
do: Keep using the chat tool for the **odd difficult email** and work as I do now.
Keep putting **a few hundred** a month into the index fund.
Ask my manager about a **senior buyer** role next year.
feel: **Settled**, like a forecast saying no storm this week.
S0.quote: A tool that saves me an hour a week doesn't change that I'm paid to negotiate and know which supplier will actually deliver.
fieldNote: Her security rests on **eight months saved**, plenty of nearby jobs and work she sees as judgement.
Her only standing worry is **rent** and wanting to buy a flat before thirty.
She sees small AI gains as freeing time for the **phone work** she enjoys.

steps.text: Keep buying gloves and soap the usual way, with AI for awkward emails
Put a few hundred a month into the index fund
Ask her manager about a senior buyer role next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to bring workers along, with training on paid time, not just switch things on. I'd be the one asking HR what the plan is for the buying team. Online I'd share stuff about unions in warehousing and offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes a lot and the team shrinks. Comparing quotes and chasing prices is exactly what these systems are good at, so maybe three buyers do what six buyers do now. I'd want to be one of the three, and right now I'm average, so that's not guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using the chat tool now and then and start using the company's system properly, once a couple of colleagues show it works. I'd ask for training and take the supplier risk side, the part that needs judgement when a factory goes quiet. And I'd hold my savings and stop the flat search for a year until I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not a disaster. There'd be lots of buying jobs around for a while, they'd just look different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your team would shrink. Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, who's 58 and does all our paper products. He's brilliant with suppliers but he still prints his emails. I'd worry he gets pushed out first, and that nobody fights for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's not a disaster. But you'd also be changing a lot. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. It's not a disaster for me, because I have savings and could find another buying job. But it's still my income that could shrink, and that's why I'd change a lot before someone changes it for me.

say: I'd say companies must offer **training on paid time**, not just switch systems on.
I'd ask HR what the **plan for buyers** is and share posts about office unions.
think: Comparing quotes is exactly what these systems do well, so the **team shrinks**.
Maybe **three buyers** do the work of six, and as an average buyer I'm not guaranteed a seat.
do: Learn the **company's buying system** properly once a couple of colleagues show it works.
Ask to take on **supplier risk**, the part that needs judgement when a factory goes quiet.
Pause the **flat search** for a year and leave the savings alone.
feel: **Nervous**, though not a disaster, since buying jobs would still be around.
S1.quote: Maybe three buyers do what six buyers do now. I'd want to be one of the three, and right now I'm average, so that's not guaranteed.
fieldNote: She expects real **job cuts** in her team and knows she could be cut, hence anxious.
Her steady style shows: she'll adopt the system **after colleagues** prove it.
Her concern for **Tomasz**, an older colleague, ties into her progressive view of fairness.

steps.text: Learn the company's buying system after two colleagues trial it
Ask to move onto supplier risk for the hospital accounts
Put the flat search on hold for a year
Raise the buying team's training plan with HR and the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments to step in, with a tax on the AI firms and income support for everyone who loses work. I'd go on marches for it. I'd tell my friends this isn't something we can each fix on our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. My job is almost all thinking work, emails and quotes and judgement calls, so I'd expect it gone within a year or so of 2028. The only safe bit is the hands-on stuff like checking a glove sample in a hospital stores room, and that's not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop all big spending and add to savings while I still earn. I'd look at work that's mostly hands-on, maybe in hospital stores or logistics, because the robots only come about 3 years after the AI. I'd join a union now and push for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor dropping. I'd feel stupid for having been proud of my job, and angry that nobody prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first week after hearing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my parents and tell them I might need to move home for a bit. Then I'd sit down with my bank statements and cancel every subscription I don't need. And I'd email the hospital stores manager I deal with, Grace, and ask if they're hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got eight months saved. How long does that really last here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year if I'm careful and cancel everything. Longer if I move back to my parents' place, which I'd hate but would do. Everyone else in buying would be looking for the same hands-on jobs at the same time, and eight months of savings goes fast then.

say: I'd say governments must **tax AI firms** and give income support to people who lose work.
I'd tell friends this isn't something we can **fix on our own**, and I'd march for it.
think: My work is almost all **thinking work**, so I'd expect it gone within a year of 2028.
Checking a **glove sample** in a stores room is the only hands-on part, and that's not a job.
do: Cancel every **subscription** I don't need and add to savings while I still earn.
Ask the **hospital stores** manager about jobs, since robots arrive about 3 years later.
Join a **union** now and push for a basic income.
feel: Like the **floor dropping**, and stupid for having been proud of my job.
S2.quote: Everyone else in buying would be looking for the same hands-on jobs at the same time, and eight months of savings goes fast then.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** around 2028, so even strong savings don't keep her calm.
She sees the **3-year robot gap** as her best bridge, through hospital stores or logistics.
Moving back to her **parents** is her fallback, which she'd hate but accept.

steps.text: Cancel unneeded subscriptions and cut spending to the basics
Ask Grace at the hospital stores about hands-on jobs
Join a union pushing for a basic income
Talk to her parents about moving home if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get it right, so let's not waste them like we did with climate. I'd want the union and the government at the table now, not in 2030. I'd be quite loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same end for my buying job, just later. Like the fast one, my work is thinking work, so 2031 is my date. But five years is enough to move into something real, and I'd be 32, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year using every AI tool at work, so I understand it, and the next year retraining. I'd use my savings to do a part-time course without quitting. I'd still keep the hospital contacts warm because I like that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I had some control. Five years is a plan, two years is a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change careers. What specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something in hospital supply chain, maybe managing stores on a ward, because it's half hands-on and half people. Or infection control, which my friend Amal does. Both need a person in the room for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you feel about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want it, but I'd buy somewhere small and cheap, near a hospital, so I'm not stuck with a big mortgage if things go wrong. Five years makes me careful, not frozen.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get it right, so let's not waste them like climate.
I'd want the **union and government** at the table now, not in 2030.
think: My buying job still **ends in 2031**, because it's thinking work.
Five years is enough to **move into something real**, and I'd only be 32.
do: Use every **AI tool at work** for the first year, so I understand it.
Pay for a **part-time course** in hospital supply out of savings without quitting.
Buy a **small, cheap flat** near a hospital rather than take a big mortgage.
feel: **Worried**, but with some control, since five years is a plan and two is a scramble.
S3.quote: Five years is a plan, two years is a scramble.
fieldNote: She still expects her **job to go**, but the extra time turns fear into a plan.
Her chosen path is **hybrid**: hospital stores or infection control, half hands-on, half people.
Housing decisions bend to the risk: **smaller flat**, smaller mortgage.

steps.text: Use the AI buying tools daily for the first year
Start a part-time course in hospital stores management
Buy a small flat near a hospital with a modest mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to build proper support, and I'd expect them to. I'd say it at work and online. If they waste it, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, more or less. I'd keep buying for five or six years and move before it lands, and my savings give me room. It still nags me, because I've seen how slowly bosses move until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep saving, and buy the flat in the next couple of years like I planned. Around year four I'd start a hospital supply course in the evenings. I'd join the union now so it's strong by the time it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit like knowing a lease ends in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much now, honestly, apart from the union. I'd stop telling myself I'll stay a buyer forever, which I sort of thought I would. Thinking about it, that's a bigger change than it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, first. My dad worked in a print shop when computers came in, and he'd tell me to have a second skill ready before I need it. He moved into the warehouse back then and never looked back.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for governments to build **proper support**.
If they waste the decade, I'd say **that's on them**.
think: I'd be **more or less fine**, buying for five or six years and moving before it lands.
It nags me, because bosses move slowly until the **last minute**.
do: Keep my job and **buy the flat** in the next couple of years.
Start an **evening course** in hospital supply around year four.
Join the **union** now so it's strong when it matters.
feel: Mostly **okay**, like knowing a lease ends in ten years.
S4.quote: My dad worked in a print shop when computers came in, and he'd tell me to have a second skill ready before I need it.
fieldNote: Ten years leaves her **income safe** for now, though the change is never far from mind.
Her father's **print shop** story shapes her plan to keep a second skill ready.
The biggest shift is mental: dropping the idea of being a **buyer forever**.

steps.text: Keep buying cleaning supplies for the distributor for now
Buy a flat in the next two years as planned
Start an evening hospital supply course around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be one of thousands of buyers looking for hands-on jobs at once. What would help is income support while I retrain, and a union with real power, so it isn't just me against the company. Cheap or free courses for hospital and care work would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who decides. Every picture assumes the companies just do it, and that's a choice, not the weather. I'd like someone to ask workers before switching on a system that does our jobs.

headlineQuote: Every picture assumes the companies just do it, and that's a choice, not the weather.
portrait: Rosa is **27**, buying cleaning and hygiene supplies for hospitals, schools and office cleaners.
She lives alone, renting, with **eight months saved** and a small index fund.
She uses AI **now and then** and would adopt new systems once colleagues prove them.
She's calm in the plateau and **alarmed** under fast AGI, expecting her thinking-heavy job to go.
With more time she plans a move into **hospital supply**, and backs unions and income support throughout.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because she'd be one of **thousands of buyers** seeking hands-on jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while she retrains, plus cheap courses for hospital and care work.
A **union with real power** and a say before systems replace workers.
